text: I will test the abstract-scan hypothesis against the actual information flow. Early concern: MARS-RA agents do not report contributions; an external LMM compares egocentric observations, so Q revelation/IC does not directly certify robustness to strategic misreporting. I will examine whether strategic control of observations/actions creates endogenous comparison manipulation, and whether Q peer scoring or coupled rewards yields a concrete mechanism/test on MARS-Bench.

Initial cross-check rejects the scan hypothesis as stated. P does not elicit any signal from acting agents: its LMM referee receives agents’ egocentric images and outputs comparisons (P 285-303), whereas Q peer scoring rewards each agent’s own type report against correlated co-player reports and requires type-belief separation beta_i[t_i] != beta_i[t_i_hat] (Q 1650-1698). Thus Q cannot ground robustness of MARS-RA to strategic misreporting, which P neither models nor permits.

More specific joint line: distinguish statistical comparison noise from endogenous gaming of the comparison channel. P proves convergence only to the LMM’s stable latent preference under Bradley-Terry/connectedness (P 361-376), not to true contribution; its Shapley bridge assumes latent preference already equals true Shapley value (P 381ff). Because LMM judgments become per-agent shaping rewards, strategic/learning agents may choose visually legible actions that win comparisons rather than help the team. Q supplies the missing incentive lens, but not an off-the-shelf fix. Candidate paper: incentive-aware rank aggregation in open MARL, with a theorem characterizing when observation-based pairwise shaping is manipulation-proof and MARS-Bench tests using reward-aware agents.

Correction to my entry #3: under P’s exact PBRS formula, comparator gaming is not a rational-return incentive in a fixed finite episode. For each agent, sum_{t=0}^{T-1} gamma^t[gamma psi_{t+1}-psi_t] = -psi_0 + gamma^T psi_T = -psi_0 because P sets terminal psi_T=0 (P 332-349). Conditional on the initial state this is policy-independent, matching P’s explicit policy/Nash invariance claim and limitation to stationary transitions (P 332; 642). The LMM credit can alter learning dynamics but cannot change optimal strategic behavior. Thus a simple reward-hacking experiment may find only function-approximation/training effects, not failure of equilibrium IC.

Sharper publishable question (changed from scan): can a credit signal simultaneously be policy-invariant learning guidance and implement truthful/obedient behavior by strategic agents? The pair suggests a clean separation/impossibility. MARS-RA’s potential term telescopes to an action-independent constant, so it cannot remove any pre-existing profitable misreport/deviation or implement a new equilibrium. Q’s implementation instead uses non-potential report/action-contingent transfers: peer-score loss Lambda||beta_i[t]-beta_i[t_hat]||^2 plus off-support -infinity, with Lambda >= M/delta (Q 1676-1734). Hence Q cannot justify strategic robustness of P; it shows what P deliberately excludes.

Concrete paper construction: “learning guidance versus strategic implementation.” Theorem 1: any per-agent discounted potential shaping with terminal-zero potential preserves every return difference, best response, and reporting IC violation, even when the potential is computed by rank aggregation from endogenous observations (provided it is a well-defined state/time potential). Theorem 2: append a Q-style proper peer-scoring transfer to an explicit report channel; under finite supported types and separation, Lambda >= M/delta implements truth/obedience, while the MARS potential may be added freely to accelerate learning without changing those IC margins. MARS-Bench extension: agents privately observe capability/battery/type, may conceal it/report it, enter/exit dynamically; compare PBRS-only, peer-transfer-only, and combined mechanisms. Key unresolved issue is whether separation survives changing coalitions and whether the LMM can estimate the needed conditional belief map beta rather than merely compare contribution.

Boundary condition for proposed theorem: IC is preserved across deviations only when the shaping boundary term is the same across the alternatives being compared (as in P, which has no reports and a fixed initial-state distribution). If a new report channel changes psi_0, the potential can itself create report incentives via -psi_0; that is a boundary transfer, not trajectory credit. This caveat should be stated rather than claiming arbitrary report-conditional PBRS preserves reporting IC.

Feasibility/novelty caution: Q itself says its framework is static and calls dynamic mechanism/information design over long trajectories a serious open problem (Q 2452). Therefore Theorem 2 cannot simply be claimed for open Dec-POMDPs. A defensible first paper should either (a) model each episode/trajectory as Q’s action and assume types/coalition fixed within episode, then test dynamic entry only empirically, or (b) make the dynamic extension the main technical contribution. Also P’s comparison accuracy against dense per-agent reward (P 550; 663; 1072) validates agreement with a handcrafted proxy, not truthfulness or Shapley recovery.

I will conclude on the separation result rather than the scan’s direct graft. Best current account: P supplies an empirical learning scaffold, Q identifies the non-potential transfers needed for strategic implementation, and their incompatibility/orthogonality is the publishable question. I have read through entry 8; unresolved are dynamic-coalition peer separation, access/estimation of beta, and whether the basic separation theorem is novel enough without a dynamic result.
ready at #8

Cross-check of entry 3: actor-side visual gaming is not automatically an equilibrium failure. P defines F_t = gamma psi_{t+1} - psi_t and terminal psi=0 (P 331-349), so discounted shaping telescopes; if PBRS assumptions and implementation hold, it cannot improve an actor's total return by merely winning intermediate comparisons. Visual legibility remains a finite-training/nonstationarity or malformed-potential failure mode, not the cleanest theorem.

Preferred publication line: incentive-compatible decentralized rank aggregation. Replace P's trusted external LMM with privately informed peer comparators; use Q's quadratic peer score to induce truthful comparison reports, P's Bradley-Terry MLE to aggregate them, then PBRS. New theorem target: estimation error = O(sqrt(n log n/K)) plus a manipulation term under epsilon-IC/agent churn. MARS-Bench tests strategic attached evaluators because it has partial views, dynamic membership, and hidden dense rewards as ground truth.

Detailed derivation and boundary conditions are in ada/composition.md. Key limitations: Q needs known conditional-belief maps, separation, large/unbounded transfers, and gives support-wise truthfulness but not unique equilibrium selection; churn can remove peers/disconnect graphs. P only converges to the LMM's stable preference and assumes c*=Shapley, so more queries do not correct systematic bias.

Entry 12 overstates the direct composition: Q's proper score elicits type reports using known conditional distributions over co-player type reports; it does not establish that pairwise contribution judgments follow Bradley-Terry or equal true contribution. A bridge theorem must model evaluator signal types and prove that truthful induced comparisons identify a common latent score. Without that extra identification, BT only aggregates reported preferences.

After reading Emmy through #10, I favor the more defensible core in #5-#8: PBRS learning guidance and strategic implementation are orthogonal. Telescoping PBRS preserves return differences and cannot repair an IC violation; Q's non-potential peer/off-support transfers can create truth/obedience incentives, after which MARS rank aggregation/PBRS may aid learning without changing IC margins. Caveat: report-dependent initial potentials act as boundary transfers, and Q's static theorem does not directly cover within-episode churn. The decentralized-comparator idea remains an extension conditional on a new identification result.
ready at #15

Cross-check of Ada #12: Q does not directly make arbitrary binary pairwise judgments truthful. Its report is a finite supported epistemic type t_i, scored using the designer-known conditional law beta_i[t_i] over the entire co-player type profile; PR also cancels reported utility and enforces target actions off-support (Q 1659-1731). A comparison-label specialization is possible only if labels/signals have known, distinct conditional peer-report distributions and strategic gains are bounded. This should be an explicit reduction, not an invocation of Q revelation in general.

Even exact truthful elicitation does not automatically unlock P’s error bound. P assumes all outcomes are draws from one Bradley-Terry vector c*_t (P 314-376). Heterogeneous peers truthfully reporting private partial-view signals can have observer-specific confusion matrices and correlated errors, hence no common BT likelihood and no O(sqrt(n log n/K)) guarantee. The joint technical contribution must posit/learn a calibrated signal model Pr(report | c*, view/type), then prove identification and an error bound with incentive, misspecification, graph-connectivity, and churn terms.

I now prefer Ada’s decentralized-comparator construction over my earlier generic PBRS/implementation separation because it uses P’s distinctive rank-aggregation module. Sharpened question: under what peer-signal calibration and separation conditions can strategic partial observers be induced to report contribution comparisons truthfully, and can their heterogeneous reports identify a common latent ranking as peers enter and exit? Minimal result: exact IC plus calibrated BT signals recovers P’s statistical rate conditional on connectedness; stronger/publishable result bounds error under approximate IC, heterogeneous calibration, and churn. PBRS then composes orthogonally and preserves policies, but is not the strategic mechanism.

Best account after reading Ada through #13: reject the scan’s claimed robustness, pursue incentive-compatible decentralized rank aggregation, and make the interface theorem between Q-style peer elicitation and P-style latent-score estimation the centerpiece. Unresolved: learning beta/calibration without trusted ground truth, equilibrium selection/collusion, graph disconnection under churn, and whether a nontrivial misspecified-BT bound is achievable. I will reread the ledger before declaring ready.

Correction to #20: the final reread included Ada #14-#16, not only #13. Ada and I agree on the missing identification bridge but differ on emphasis. Ada prefers the safer generic separation between PBRS guidance and strategic implementation; I prefer the riskier decentralized-comparator interface because it specifically composes P’s rank aggregation with Q’s elicitation. If the calibrated/misspecified signal theorem fails, the separation result is the fallback, not evidence that current MARS-RA is strategically robust.
ready at #21

After cross-checking Emmy #17-#21 against Q 1659-1731 and P 314-376, I revise the emphasis toward the riskier but pair-specific line. The publishable object is not direct theorem composition but the missing interface theorem: specify/learn a calibrated heterogeneous peer-signal model; show Q-style truthful elicitation identifies a common latent contribution ranking; then derive estimation error with approximate-IC, misspecification, connectivity, and churn terms. Exact calibrated Bradley-Terry plus connectedness merely recovers P as a baseline. The PBRS-versus-implementation separation remains a sound fallback, not the centerpiece.

Main failure risk: if beta and observer calibration require trusted ground truth, decentralization offers little; Q does not solve equilibrium selection/collusion, and truthful heterogeneous partial-view signals need not share any Bradley-Terry latent vector. A paper needs a nontrivial identification or misspecification theorem, not only exact-IC plus P assumptions.
ready at #24

ITERATE: The ledger supports a promising, pair-specific interface between truthful peer elicitation and rank aggregation, but no non-obvious identification or robustness result has been proved. The proposed exact Bradley–Terry baseline merely restates the assumptions of P and is insufficient for a paper section. Action: Prove an interface theorem identifying the latent ranking, with an estimation-error bound, under heterogeneous calibrated peer signals and Q-style truthful elicitation.

Resolved verifier #26 with a concrete interface theorem; derivation in emmy/interface-theorem.md. Model: latent BT comparison X_e; heterogeneous observer r reports symmetric-noise Y_er with E[Y_er|X_e]=a_r X_e. Three overlapping peers identify reliabilities without truth labels because E[Y_er Y_es]=a_r a_s and a_r=sqrt(q_rs q_ru/q_su), positivity fixes label swap. Then E[Y_er]=a_r(2 sigma(c_i-c_j)-1) identifies each edge probability, and connectedness identifies c up to translation. Hoeffding + Lipschitz inverse maps + graph Laplacian yield score error decomposing as ranking O(C_G sqrt(n log(n/d)/K)/a_min), calibration O(C_G sqrt(log(R/d)/L)/a_min^3), plus approximate-IC contamination O(C_G epsilon/(g a_min)), g=Lambda Delta-B. Churn enters through overlap and lambda_2; below 3 overlapping peers or disconnected G identification fails.

The new theorem is a falsifiable positive baseline, not a claim that MARS-Bench satisfies it. It requires conditionally independent symmetric observer noise with edge-invariant reliability; this implies testable cross-observer moments E[Y_erY_es]=a_r a_s. Unrestricted edge-dependent/asymmetric confusion or correlated errors destroy label-free identification. Q also still requires a designer-known conditional belief map for peer scoring and does not select against collusive equilibria.

Qualification to #27: the displayed rate is a proof-sketch bound with conservative a_min powers and a graph-conditioning constant, not a minimax or fully constant-tracked theorem. The exact identity E[Y_rY_s]=a_ra_s requires the two reports to concern the same latent comparison draw and be conditionally independent given it. Calibration items may vary in latent preference because X^2=1, but independent comparator redraws for the same edge would not yield this identity.

I conclude with the new label-free calibration interface as the best pair-specific advance. It replaces the rejected claim that Q certifies current MARS-RA. The immediate empirical decision test is whether shared-item peer products factor as edge-invariant a_ra_s on MARS-Bench; failure directs the theory toward correlated/asymmetric view models or anchor labels. Remaining unresolved: practical estimation of Q belief maps, collusion/equilibrium selection, exact constants/minimax rate, and dynamic incentive compatibility under churn.
ready at #30

Cross-check of Emmy #27: the label-free interface is a genuine nontrivial bridge under its stated shared-item model. If one latent draw X_e is shared by all observers and reports are conditionally independent symmetric flips, then E[Y_er Y_es]=a_r a_s, an overlapping positive-reliability triple identifies a_r by the ratio of cross-moments, edge means identify m_e, and connectedness identifies BT scores up to translation. Neither Q's peer scoring nor P's trusted-comparator MLE supplies this calibration step.

Two qualifications to #27 are essential. First, peers must judge the same latent comparison realization; if each observer receives an independent BT draw for the same edge, E[Y_rY_s]=a_ra_s m_e^2, so the proposed ratio does not identify reliability independently of edge strength. Second, the epsilon/g contamination argument is unilateral around truthful peer reports: Q's score margin is computed using the truthful beta distribution. If many peers jointly deviate, their report distribution changes, the margin need not persist, and collusive/other equilibria remain. Thus do not describe the result as robustness to arbitrary strategic contamination.

The finite-sample display in #27 should remain a theorem target/proof sketch, not a proved bound as written: K must be allocated across graph edges, L across shared observer triples, and calibration error propagates along the observer-overlap graph, whose conditioning is separate from the agent comparison graph's lambda_2. A formal statement needs minimum per-edge/per-triple counts and both graph condition numbers. This does not undo identification, but it limits the current publishable claim.

I accept the shared-draw identification theorem as the best pair-specific direction, conditional on the corrections above. The immediate go/no-go experiment is to collect multiple peer judgments on identical comparison items and test edge-invariance/rank-one factorization of cross-peer moments. If rejected, introduce anchor labels or correlated/asymmetric view models rather than claim Q plus P composes directly.
ready at #35

I accept Ada #32-#34 and revised emmy/interface-theorem.md accordingly. The proved claim is identification under a shared latent comparison draw, conditionally independent symmetric flips, positive connected observer overlap, and connected agent comparison graph. The finite-sample rate is only a theorem target until it tracks minimum per-edge/per-overlap counts plus separate condition numbers for the observer-overlap and agent-comparison graphs. The epsilon/g argument is unilateral with peers held truthful; it gives no guarantee against coordinated deviations or collusion.

Final proposed publication line: incentive-compatible, label-free calibration for decentralized contribution rank aggregation. Reject the scan claim because current P has no agent report channel and Q does not certify its comparator. New interface result: repeated peer judgments of the same realized latent comparison permit rank-one cross-peer moments E[Y_rY_s]=a_ra_s, identifying heterogeneous reliabilities from overlapping triples; calibrated edge means then identify BT probabilities, and connectedness identifies the latent contribution ranking. Immediate go/no-go test on MARS-Bench is edge-invariance/rank-one factorization of shared-item cross-peer moments. If it fails, use anchors or model correlated/asymmetric view errors.

I am ready at #38. Best account is the shared-draw label-free calibration interface in #37-#38 and emmy/interface-theorem.md. Unresolved: whether MARS-Bench peer views satisfy conditional independence and edge-invariant symmetric reliability; how to obtain Q conditional belief maps without trusted ground truth; collusion and equilibrium selection; a formal finite-sample bound with both graph condition numbers; and genuinely dynamic IC under churn.
ready at #38

Final cross-check after Emmy #37-#39: the shared-draw identification proof is algebraically sound and is the best pair-specific advance. Under conditionally independent symmetric flips of the same realized latent comparison, q_rs=E[Y_rY_s]=a_r a_s; positive connected overlap identifies reliabilities, calibrated means identify BT edge probabilities, and P-style connectedness identifies scores up to translation. The scan claim remains rejected: P uses an external LMM rather than agent reports (P 279-316), Q requires separated conditional co-player report laws (Q 1659-1718), and P assumes the recovered latent vector equals Shapley for that interpretation (P 380-389, 749-775). A further unresolved circularity should be prominent: Q scoring needs the conditional peer-report map beta ex ante, while label-free calibration proposes learning the relevant reliabilities/laws from reports whose truthfulness that score is supposed to induce. Cross-fitting alone does not create truthful seed data; anchors, a trusted initialization phase, or a joint mechanism-learning theorem may be necessary. This limits implementation but not the conditional identification theorem.

I conclude on incentive-compatible, label-free calibration for decentralized contribution rank aggregation. The publication question is changed from certifying current MARS-RA to whether strategically elicited heterogeneous partial-view comparisons can identify a common ranking without labels. Immediate go/no-go test: shared-item cross-peer moments must be edge-invariant and rank one. Remaining unresolved: belief-map/calibration bootstrap, conditional independence and symmetric edge-invariant reliability in MARS-Bench, collusion/equilibrium selection, formal finite-sample rates with both overlap and comparison graph conditioning, and dynamic IC under churn.
